title: Quadratic Residues and the Legendre Symbol

items.title: Quadratic residues and nonresidues modulo an integer
Quadratic residuosity is representative-independent and the residues are the image of squaring
items.strategy: Translate congruence through equality in the quotient ring. If $[x]^2=[a]$ and $[a]$ is a unit, then $[x]$ is a unit because an inverse of $[x]^2$ gives one for $[x]$; thus every residue witness lies in the unit group. Congruent representatives share the same witnesses, and conversely every value of unit-group squaring satisfies the defining congruence.

items.title: A coprime exponent gives a unique nonzero $k$-th root modulo a prime
items.strategy: Specialise the published binomial-congruence criterion and solution count using $\varphi(p)=p-1$ and the existence of primitive roots. If $k\ell\equiv1\pmod{p-1}$, Fermat's theorem verifies that $a^\ell$ is a root; another inverse exponent differs by a multiple of $p-1$, so the displayed root is representative-independent.

items.title: The nonzero squares modulo an odd prime form an index-two subgroup
items.strategy: Select one primitive root for the fixed prime and write every unit as a power of it. Division by two in the exponent shows that the intrinsic image of squaring is exactly $\langle g^2\rangle$ and has the two cosets of even and odd powers. The subgroup itself is independent of the selected generator.

items.title: An odd prime has $(p-1)/2$ nonzero quadratic residues and as many nonresidues
items.strategy: Apply Lagrange's theorem to the index-two square subgroup. For a square target, specialise the published binomial-congruence solution count at exponent two to obtain exactly two square roots; for a nonsquare target there are none.

items.title: The Legendre symbol, including its zero value
The Legendre symbol is well defined on residue classes
items.strategy: Split exhaustively according as the prime divides the numerator. Divisibility and, in the unit case, quadratic residuosity are unchanged on replacing the numerator by a congruent integer, so exactly one of the values zero, one, and minus one applies.

items.title: On the units, the Legendre symbol is the unique nontrivial homomorphism to $\{\pm1\}$
items.strategy: Use the quotient of the cyclic unit group by its square subgroup: even powers map to one and odd powers to minus one, making the kernel exactly the squares and the map surjective. Any nontrivial homomorphism must send a selected primitive root to minus one and is therefore identical. The selection is local to the fixed prime.

items.title: Euler's criterion: $(a/p)\equiv a^{(p-1)/2}\pmod p$
items.strategy: Handle $p\mid a$ first. For a unit, the published power-residue criterion identifies squares with the value one. Fermat's theorem makes the half-power a root of $X^2-1$; the root bound over the field $\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z$ leaves only one and minus one, and the nonsquare case must be minus one.

items.title: The Legendre symbol is multiplicative for all integer numerators
items.strategy: If the prime divides either factor, both sides are zero. Otherwise pass to the two unit classes and apply the established homomorphism. As a corollary, a square factor coprime to the prime can be removed from the numerator.

items.title: $x^2\equiv a\pmod p$ has exactly $1+(a/p)$ solution classes
items.strategy: Use three exhaustive Legendre-symbol cases. A nonzero square has two roots by the published binomial-congruence count, a nonresidue has none by definition, and when $p\mid a$ the field equation $x^2=0$ forces the unique zero class.

items.title: The discriminant counts roots of $Ax^2+Bx+C\equiv0\pmod p$ for odd prime $p\nmid A$
items.strategy: Multiply the congruence by $4A$ and complete the square to obtain $(2Ax+B)^2\equiv B^2-4AC$. Since $p\nmid2A$, the affine change $x\mapsto2Ax+B$ is a bijection on residue classes; apply the quadratic solution-count formula to the discriminant.

items.title: Multiplication permutes an odd prime's signed half-system up to sign
items.strategy: For each $1\le j\le(p-1)/2$, take the unique standard representative of $aj$ and replace it by its signed representative in the half-system. Equal absolute representatives would give $j\equiv k$ or $j\equiv-k\pmod p$; the endpoint inequalities force $j=k$ in the first case and exclude the second. Finite self-injectivity then gives every absolute representative exactly once.

items.title: Gauss's quadratic-residue lemma
items.strategy: Write the signed congruence $aj\equiv\varepsilon_j r_j$ for the complete half-system, where exactly $N(a,p)$ signs are negative. Multiply all congruences, use the permutation of the absolute representatives, and cancel their nonzero product modulo $p$. Euler's criterion identifies the remaining half-power with the Legendre symbol.

items.title: First supplement: $(-1/p)=(-1)^{(p-1)/2}$
items.strategy: Substitute $a=-1$ into Euler's criterion. Divide the odd prime by four to show the exponent is even exactly for remainder one and odd exactly for remainder three, yielding the equivalent residue-class formulation.

items.title: Second supplement: $(2/p)=(-1)^{(p^2-1)/8}$
items.strategy: In Gauss's half-system for $a=2$, a sign is negative exactly when $p/4<j<p/2$. Write $p=8q+r$ with remainder one, three, five, or seven; in each case list the integer range explicitly and count it, obtaining the parity of $(p^2-1)/8$ without a floor-function dependency.

title: Quadratic Residues and the Legendre Symbol — Examples

items.title: Quadratic residues, roots, and the Legendre table modulo $11$
items.strategy: Square the five signed pairs of nonzero classes, list the residue subgroup and the two roots of each square, then tabulate the Legendre symbol on all eleven classes, including zero.

items.title: Fourth and eighth powers modulo $17$
items.strategy: Use the published power-residue criterion and solution count with exponents four and eight. Compute the target tests and list the resulting power subgroups and the exact number of roots of every soluble target.

items.title: Two quadratic nonresidues modulo $15$ can have a nonresidue product
items.strategy: List the eight unit classes modulo $15$ and square them; their square image consists only of the classes $1$ and $4$. Thus $2$, $7$, and $14$ are all quadratic nonresidues, while the product of $2$ and $7$ is congruent to $14$ modulo $15$. This isolates the failure of the prime-modulus sign rule.

items.title: The unique cube root of $2$ modulo $29$ is $-3$
items.strategy: Since $3$ is coprime to $28$, use the inverse exponent $19$ modulo $28$ in the unique-root formula. Reduce $2^{19}$ to $-3$ modulo $29$ and verify directly that $(-3)^3\equiv2\pmod{29}$.

items.title: Euler's criterion computes $(3/726377359)$ by repeated squaring
items.strategy: Compute $3^{(p-1)/2}$ modulo the prime $p=726377359$ by a displayed repeated-squaring table. Interpret the final value through Euler's criterion without factoring the numerator.

items.title: The signed half-system for $3$ modulo $11$ gives $(3/11)=1$
items.strategy: Reduce $3,6,9,12,15$ to the signed representatives $3,-5,-2,1,4$, verify their absolute values permute $1,\ldots,5$, and count two negative signs.

items.title: A nonmonic quadratic congruence solved through its discriminant
items.strategy: For $3x^2+4x+1\equiv0\pmod{11}$ compute the discriminant, use its Legendre value to predict two roots, complete the square, and recover and check both classes.

items.title: Squaring is not a homomorphism on a nonabelian group
items.strategy: In the symmetric group on three letters choose two transpositions whose product is a three-cycle. Their squares are the identity but the square of their product is not, so $g\mapsto g^2$ fails the homomorphism law outside the abelian setting.

items.title: A soluble square congruence need not define a quadratic residue
items.strategy: For every odd prime, $x^2\equiv0\pmod p$ has the unique zero solution, but zero is outside the unit residue/nonresidue dichotomy and its Legendre symbol is zero. Contrast solvability with the definition's coprimality hypothesis.
